systems.n: Abdominal Examination and Signs of Chronic Liver Disease

topics.n: Pallor and anaemia in liver disease

facts.t: **Pallor** of the conjunctivae, nail beds and palmar creases is due to a reduced haemoglobin concentration, i.e. **anaemia** until proven otherwise; investigate with a **CBC** (with MCV to classify the anaemia), liver function tests and serum albumin to look for chronic liver disease as the cause.

**Hypersplenism** from portal hypertension causes splenic sequestration of blood cells, giving **pancytopenia** (anaemia + leucopenia + thrombocytopenia); cirrhosis with splenomegaly and low haemoglobin, white cells and platelets points to hypersplenism.

Anaemia in cirrhosis is multifactorial: **iron deficiency** from gastrointestinal blood loss (varices, portal hypertensive gastropathy, peptic ulcer, **GAVE**/watermelon stomach) gives a microcytic hypochromic picture with low ferritin and positive occult blood in stool, whereas **anaemia of chronic disease** has normal or high ferritin; anorexia and poor nutrition also contribute, while ascites does not cause anaemia.

Bilateral **pitting oedema** has three classic causes: **heart** (right-sided heart failure, with raised JVP), **liver** (cirrhosis, with ascites and low albumin) and **kidney** (nephrotic syndrome); in cirrhosis the mechanism is decreased plasma oncotic pressure from **hypoalbuminaemia** plus portal hypertension and sodium/water retention, and the oedema is gravity-dependent, worse by evening and better overnight, with a normal JVP.

**Pitting oedema** is soft and compressible, leaves a pit on pressure and often has shiny overlying skin; **lymphoedema** is typically firm and non-pitting, **unilateral** leg swelling suggests **DVT** until excluded, and cellulitis is red, hot and tender. Anaemia and hyperthyroidism are not classic causes of leg oedema.

A **spider naevus** (spider angioma, venous star) is a central arteriole with radiating capillaries that **blanches on pressure** over the centre and refills from the centre outwards; it occurs in the SVC territory (face, chest above the nipples) and reflects **hyperoestrogenism** from impaired hepatic inactivation of oestrogen in liver cell failure. A few can be normal, but more than 5 suggests chronic liver disease.

**Palmar erythema** is redness of the palms, especially the **thenar and hypothenar eminences**, most commonly due to **liver cell failure** (hyperoestrogenism, with vascular dilatation); it also occurs in pregnancy, thyrotoxicosis and rheumatoid arthritis. The hyperoestrogenism cluster of chronic liver disease is spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia and testicular atrophy.

topics.n: Abdominal wall veins and caput medusae

facts.t: **Dilated abdominal wall veins** are portosystemic collaterals of **portal hypertension**, most commonly due to liver **cirrhosis**; **caput medusae** is the network of veins radiating from the umbilicus through recanalised paraumbilical veins, with flow away from the umbilicus (in IVC obstruction the flank veins flow upwards). Collaterals also form when a major vein is obstructed or thrombosed, and Budd-Chiari syndrome is a less common cause.

topics.n: Abdominal distension and ascites on examination

facts.t: Generalised abdominal distension with **bulging flanks** is **ascites** until proven otherwise, confirmed by **shifting dullness** (about 1.5 L of fluid needed) and a fluid wave/fluid thrill; the commonest cause is liver **cirrhosis**, and ascites with hypoalbuminaemia and a prolonged INR means decompensated disease. Ultrasound confirms free fluid and the state of the liver.
**Cullen's sign** is periumbilical ecchymosis (bruising around the umbilicus), seen in acute haemorrhagic pancreatitis and in ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

**Diastasis (divarication) of the recti** is a widening of the linea alba giving a midline supra-umbilical bulge or ridge that appears on coughing, straining or raising the head, with a palpable separation of the rectus muscles and **no discrete hernial defect**; it results from raised intra-abdominal pressure plus a weak wall (repeated pregnancy, ascites, obesity, chronic cough, organomegaly, weak muscles) and is usually painless.

Abdominal **striae** result from prolonged stretching of the skin by repeated pregnancy, ascites, organomegaly (including huge splenomegaly), obesity and Cushing's syndrome; they are initially red/purple (**striae rubrae**) and later turn silvery (albicans). Acute illness such as viral hepatitis, acute diarrhoea or chronic constipation does not cause striae.

**Tender hepatomegaly** results from stretching of Glisson's capsule in a **congested liver** (right-sided heart failure), **acute hepatitis** and **liver abscess**; chronic hepatitis C and advanced cirrhosis (a small, shrunken, firm liver) give non-tender enlargement.

**Hepatosplenomegaly** means enlargement of both the liver and the spleen; common adult causes are **chronic hepatitis C** with portal hypertension, **haemolytic anaemia**, malaria, lymphoma and leukaemia. Work-up includes CBC, liver function tests, serology for viral hepatitis and ultrasound.

systems.n: Upper GI Bleeding, Ascites and Portal Hypertension

facts.t: In **haematemesis**, **resuscitation** comes first (airway, breathing, circulation: IV access, fluids/blood, oxygen), then drugs (PPI, or terlipressin/octreotide if varices are suspected), then **endoscopy** once the patient is stabilised; a gastric wash has no role. In haemorrhagic shock, management is resuscitation plus blood transfusion (cautiously, target Hb about 7-8 g/dL in variceal bleeding, as over-transfusion raises portal pressure) plus endoscopy, and the initial laboratory investigation is a **complete blood picture** to assess blood loss.

The commonest cause of **ascites** by far is liver **cirrhosis** (portal hypertension plus hypoalbuminaemia); other causes include right-sided heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, malignancy/peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculous peritonitis, Budd-Chiari syndrome and Meigs' syndrome (ovarian fibroma with ascites and right pleural effusion). Anaemia, acute diarrhoea and HIV infection itself do not cause ascites.

The **serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG)** separates causes: **SAAG >= 1.1 g/dL** indicates portal hypertension, while < 1.1 g/dL indicates peritoneal causes (malignancy, tuberculosis). High SAAG with **low ascitic protein** (< 2.5 g/dL) points to cirrhosis, high SAAG with high protein points to a cardiac cause or Budd-Chiari syndrome, and nephrotic syndrome gives a low SAAG.

**Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)** is diagnosed by paracentesis showing ascitic neutrophils (PMNs) **>= 250 cells/mm3**; bacterial cultures are often negative, the commonest organisms are **Gram-negative** (E. coli, Klebsiella), and treatment is IV **cefotaxime** plus albumin, with norfloxacin for secondary prophylaxis.

**Portal hypertension** in cirrhosis results from increased resistance to portal blood flow within the liver; its manifestations are ascites, splenomegaly, caput medusae, oesophageal varices and haematemesis/melaena. **Portal vein thrombosis** is the commonest pre-hepatic cause of portal hypertension.

**Oesophageal varices** appear on upper endoscopy as bluish, tortuous cords protruding into the lumen of the lower oesophagus; **cherry-red spots** (red wale marks) mark a high risk of bleeding. Bleeding varices present with haematemesis of bright red blood with or without melaena, pallor, hypotension and tachycardia.

Acute variceal bleeding is treated with resuscitation, a vasoactive drug (terlipressin/octreotide), antibiotics and endoscopic **variceal band ligation**, which is the treatment of choice at endoscopy; biopsy of varices is dangerous. **Primary prophylaxis** of varices that have never bled is a **non-selective beta-blocker** (propranolol/carvedilol) or band ligation, and secondary prophylaxis after a bleed is both.

**Helicobacter pylori** infection is the most common cause of **peptic ulcer** disease (found in the large majority of duodenal ulcers): it colonises the gastric antrum, causing chronic inflammation with **lymphoid follicles** and later gastric gland atrophy, which weakens mucosal defence and leads to ulceration. Eradication (PPI plus two antibiotics) prevents recurrence.

**NSAIDs** are the second common cause of peptic ulcer: COX-1 inhibition reduces protective **prostaglandins**, mucus and bicarbonate, causing mucosal injury, ulceration and melaena. A long NSAID history points to an NSAID ulcer; management is to stop the NSAID if possible, give a PPI and test for H. pylori.

A **gastric ulcer** is typically a single, clean-based ulcer on the **lesser curvature** of the stomach; always **biopsy** the edge to exclude carcinoma and repeat endoscopy after healing (8-12 weeks), and test for and eradicate H. pylori.

A **duodenal ulcer** is typically a single, clean-based ulcer in the **duodenal bulb**; initial management is **proton pump inhibitor** therapy for 4-8 weeks plus removal of the cause (NSAID or H. pylori).

Diarrhoea is classified by duration: **acute** diarrhoea lasts **< 2 weeks** (usually infective), **persistent** diarrhoea 2-4 weeks, and **chronic** diarrhoea **> 4 weeks**, which needs investigation.

In **chronic diarrhoea**, look for oedema and ascites (**protein-losing enteropathy**), **weight loss**, signs of dehydration and hypovolaemia, and signs of **fat-soluble vitamin deficiency** (A, D, E, K) or steatorrhoea from malabsorption; weight gain, hypertension and jaundice are not typical features.

**Crohn's disease** is characterised by **transmural inflammation** with **skip lesions**, deep longitudinal ulcers and a **cobblestone appearance**, and non-caseating **granulomas** on biopsy; it can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus, most often the terminal ileum and right colon, presenting with abdominal pain, diarrhoea with or without blood or mucus, weight loss, right lower quadrant tenderness or mass, and mouth ulcers.

Crohn's disease forms **perianal fistulae** and abscesses (ulcerative colitis does not) and has extra-intestinal manifestations including aphthous mouth ulcers, **arthritis/arthralgia**, erythema nodosum, uveitis and skin rashes.

**Ulcerative colitis** is **continuous mucosal inflammation** starting at the **rectum** and extending proximally without skip areas, limited to the colon and rectum, with **crypt abscesses** on biopsy; it presents with bloody diarrhoea with mucus, urgency and abdominal cramping. A **lead-pipe colon** on barium enema and pseudopolyps with superficial ulceration are ulcerative colitis features.

**Colonoscopy with mucosal biopsy** is the gold standard for diagnosing inflammatory bowel disease, distinguishing ulcerative colitis from Crohn's disease and excluding infection and malignancy. Deep colonic ulcers present with bleeding per rectum, diarrhoea and abdominal pain, and chronic blood loss causes **iron deficiency anaemia**, the common haematological complication (vitamin B12 deficiency occurs with terminal ileal Crohn's disease).

**Conjugated (direct) bilirubin** reflects the **excretory function** of the liver (secretion into bile); serum albumin and total protein reflect **synthetic function**, **alkaline phosphatase** (with GGT) is a cholestatic enzyme, and ALT/AST reflect hepatocellular injury.

**Abdominal ultrasound** is the best **first-line investigation** for liver disease and for jaundice: it detects focal lesions, bile duct dilatation, stones, masses, cirrhosis and ascites. Dilated bile ducts point to obstructive jaundice, while no dilatation points to an intrahepatic cause; CT/MRI, liver biopsy and ERCP are second-line.

**Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia** occurs in **haemolysis** (acholuric jaundice, no bilirubin in urine) and in familial hyperbilirubinaemias (**Gilbert**, Crigler-Najjar, Dubin-Johnson syndrome), while predominantly **conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia** occurs in bile duct obstruction, drug-induced liver injury and primary biliary cholangitis. Scleral icterus appears at a bilirubin of about 2.5-3 mg/dL, and anaemia alone never causes jaundice.

**Hepatocellular jaundice** is a mixed direct and indirect hyperbilirubinaemia with raised **ALT/AST**, hepatomegaly and right upper quadrant tenderness, caused by impaired conjugation and excretion of bilirubin by damaged hepatocytes, with no biliary obstruction on ultrasound.

**Obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice** gives predominantly **conjugated bilirubin** with raised **alkaline phosphatase**, dark urine (bilirubinuria), pale stools and itching; colicky right hypochondrial pain after fatty meals with a calculous gallbladder and dilated ducts points to **choledocholithiasis**. Charcot's triad (pain, fever, jaundice) suggests ascending cholangitis.

On ultrasound, **cirrhosis** shows a **small, shrunken, nodular liver** with irregular margins and coarse echotexture/increased echogenicity, often with **splenomegaly** and ascites; a nodular liver edge is the characteristic finding.

**Decompensated** liver disease is marked by **ascites**, jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy and variceal bleeding, with impaired synthetic function shown by **low albumin** and a prolonged prothrombin time/INR; hepatomegaly and a raised ALT alone do not indicate decompensation.

Complications of cirrhosis include **spontaneous bacterial peritonitis**, **hepatocellular carcinoma** (the key risk in chronic hepatitis B, which can cause HCC even without cirrhosis) and hepatorenal syndrome; cirrhosis causes **thrombocytopenia** from hypersplenism and low thrombopoietin, never thrombocytosis, and a falling platelet count suggests portal hypertension. Patients with HBV/HCV cirrhosis need HCC surveillance with ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months.

**Hepatitis A** spreads by the **faecal-oral route** through contaminated water and food; the illness is acute and self-limiting, usually mild to moderate and worse in adults than in children, and **never becomes chronic**. **IgM anti-HAV** marks acute infection, a vaccine is available, and the keyed histology is ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes with Councilman (acidophilic) bodies.

In **hepatitis B**, **HBsAg** means infection, not immunity (immunity is **anti-HBs**); **IgM anti-HBc** marks **acute** infection, and **HBeAg** positivity means active viral replication and **high infectivity**. HBV spreads by blood, sexual and vertical transmission, not faecal-orally, and a vaccine exists.

Chronic active **hepatitis B** (raised ALT with high **HBV DNA**, with or without fibrosis) is treated with antiviral therapy with **tenofovir** or entecavir, which have a high barrier to resistance; corticosteroids can flare HBV. Histology shows interface hepatitis with lymphocytic infiltration and hepatocyte necrosis, and **ground-glass hepatocytes** in chronic infection.

**Hepatitis C** is transmitted mainly by **blood-to-blood (parenteral) contact**, such as sharing needles, transfusion and unsafe injections; sexual and vertical spread are minor, and faecal-oral or respiratory spread does not occur. Diagnosis is **anti-HCV** antibodies followed by **HCV RNA (PCR)** to confirm active infection, and there is **no HCV vaccine**.

Active hepatitis C with detectable HCV RNA, even with only mild fibrosis, is treated with **direct-acting antivirals (DAAs)**, for example sofosbuvir-based regimens for 8-12 weeks, which cure over 95% (sustained virological response); watchful waiting is inappropriate.

**Acute hepatitis** can be caused by **autoimmune hepatitis**, cytomegalovirus and mushroom (Amanita) poisoning; **schistosomiasis (bilharziasis)** does not cause acute hepatitis but chronic periportal (**pipe-stem**) fibrosis with preserved liver function. Autoimmune hepatitis shows interface hepatitis with **plasma cell** infiltrates.

systems.n: Metabolic, Vascular Liver Disease and Liver Tumours

facts.t: **Budd-Chiari syndrome** is **obstruction of the hepatic veins** (hepatic outflow obstruction) causing congestion with sudden severe right upper quadrant pain, **tender hepatomegaly**, ascites, leg oedema, jaundice and dilated abdominal wall veins over days to weeks. Look for prothrombotic states such as **oral contraceptive** use, polycythaemia and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria; Doppler ultrasound shows **absent or reversed flow** in the hepatic veins.

topics.n: Hepatocellular carcinoma and focal liver lesions

facts.t: **Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)** arises in chronic **hepatitis B** (even without cirrhosis) and hepatitis C cirrhosis, presenting with weight loss, right upper quadrant pain, jaundice and a firm, irregular liver mass with raised **alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)**; a new focal lesion in a cirrhotic liver is HCC until proven otherwise, surveillance is ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months, and early solitary HCC is managed by surgical resection, ablation/transplant or locoregional therapy.

**Ultrasound** is the preferred initial imaging for HCC detection in cirrhosis, and **triphasic CT** (or MRI) characterises a focal lesion: **arterial hyper-enhancement with washout** in the portal/delayed phase is diagnostic of HCC without biopsy. Metastases are usually multiple and hypovascular, and haemangioma and focal nodular hyperplasia do not raise AFP.

**Haemangioma** is the commonest benign liver tumour: a well-circumscribed **hyperechoic** lesion on ultrasound in a patient without liver disease, histologically a proliferation of blood vessels with a **cavernous pattern**; no biopsy is needed. Focal nodular hyperplasia instead shows a central scar with malformed vessels.

topics.n: Gallstones, bile duct stones and obstructive jaundice

facts.t: A **gallbladder stone** appears on ultrasound as a mobile **echogenic focus with a posterior acoustic shadow**; biliary colic is right hypochondrial pain **referred to the right shoulder** with dyspepsia after fatty meals. Gallbladder polyps are fixed and do not shadow, and sludge (mud) does not shadow.

**Choledocholithiasis** (common bile duct stone) causes jaundice with dark urine and pale stools, right upper quadrant pain and raised bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase with a dilated common bile duct; the next step is **ERCP**, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic (sphincterotomy and stone extraction), while MRCP is non-invasive diagnosis only.

**Painless jaundice** with weight loss and dilated intra- and extra-hepatic bile ducts with no visible mass suggests a common bile duct stricture or small tumour, and is **pancreatic head cancer** until proven otherwise (Courvoisier's sign: a palpable non-tender gallbladder); **ERCP with brush cytology** and possible stenting gives a tissue diagnosis and relieves the obstruction in the same session.
